title: what a sikh carries and why
hookLine: what a Sikh carries and why
tomorrow: the tenth guru, the khalsa, the saint-soldier

lines: A RING, A PHOTO, A WATCH.
TOUCH IT, AND SOMETHING COMES BACK.
cards: A wedding ring turned during a hard meeting. A photo in a wallet. A grandmother's watch that doesn't keep time anymore.
Small things people carry to remember. They don't do anything, exactly. Touch one, and something comes back: a promise, a person, who someone meant to be.
Initiated Sikhs carry five of them, every day.

teach.h: FIVE THINGS THAT BEGIN WITH K.
teach.b: They're the five Ks, because in Punjabi each one begins with the sound k. Sikhs initiated into the Khalsa, the family that began with the five on day four, keep all five.
Kesh: uncut hair, from day three, under the turban.

teach.h: KESH AND KANGA — HAIR, AND ITS COMB.
teach.b: Kanga: a small wooden comb tucked into the hair. Keep the hair clean and ordered, and the life too.
Kara: the steel circle on the wrist, also from day three.
Kachera: a cotton undergarment, like simple shorts: self-restraint, and readiness to move. Kirpan: a small sword, worn in a sheath, often under the clothes.
It stands for the duty to protect people who can't protect themselves, and for dignity and courage. It isn't there for aggression. Notice what all five have in common.
None is a decoration. A comb, a bracelet, underwear, hair: plain, ordinary things. The reminders aren't locked away in a temple.
They're on the body, at work, at the gym, all day. Faith you can touch. Many Sikhs who aren't initiated still wear the kara, and wherever you are with the rest, this path starts from there.

how: Sikhs initiated into the Khalsa keep the five Ks at all times: uncut hair, a wooden comb, a steel bracelet, a cotton undergarment and a small sword. Many other Sikhs wear the kara.

games.q: the five Ks — tap the pairs.

s: the kirpan is a weapon for attacking
it's a symbol of the duty to protect those who can't protect themselves.
the five Ks are kept by Sikhs initiated into the Khalsa
and many Sikhs who aren't initiated still wear the kara.
the five Ks are decorations for festival days
they're plain, practical, and worn every day by initiated Sikhs.

games.q: your hand is reaching for something you'd regret. you're wearing a kara. what's it for?
o: it's jewelry. it doesn't do anything.
it's there first, asking if this is something your hand should do.
it protects you from bad luck.
games.why: Sikhs often say the kara reminds the hand of who it belongs to, before it acts.

practice: Choose one thing you're wearing or carrying: a ring, a watch, a hair tie, your sleeve. Put your hand on it and decide, just for now, what it will remind you of: something you believe, a person, a promise.
Close your hand around it and breathe with that meaning for a while.

wordCard.voice: The five Ks. Kesh, kanga, kara, kachera, kirpan: five reminders a committed Sikh carries every day. Eighteenth word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: kakar, the name for the five articles of faith that begin with k.

carryVoice: Your line: reminders you can touch. Faith that goes where you go, not left behind at the door. Day eighteen.

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada (the five kakars for initiated Sikhs)
